Who We Are

We are the Paw-cket Scientists! Represented by our adorable, high-spirited bear mascot blasting through orbit, we are a group of creative space enthusiasts ready to turn complex spacecraft engineering into an absolute blast! For this year's Space Apps Challenge, we’re taking on the Space Mission Design Game to build a fun, engaging, and strategic simulation that lets anyone become a space mission director.
summary:
Last Contact is a browser game developed by Team Pocket Scientist for NASA’s Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players take the role of mission control investigators after a spacecraft goes silent. They inspect the 3D spacecraft, reconstruct the failure using simulated flight recorder data, and check their calculations against the evidence. Then they change one design decision, predict the outcome, and run a new flight. The game evaluates spacecraft survival, science delivery, and design cost separately.

In one simulated mission, adding solar wings keeps the satellite alive, but only 51% of its planned science reaches Earth. Scheduling a radio pass every orbit raises delivery to 100% and uses more power and ground-station time. NASA mission reports and spacecraft specifications inform the investigations. The planned eight-case campaign also explores onboard storage, propulsion reliability, backup communications, telescope pointing, thermal recovery, unit checks, and command validation.

Last Contact gives students and science clubs a way to practice engineering decisions that are often taught separately. Players learn to explain why a fix works, what it costs, and whether the spacecraft can still accomplish its science objective.
details:
Last Contact

Team Pocket Scientist · NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Space Mission Design Game

A small satellite starts its mission with a full battery. Ten orbits later, it goes silent. In Last Contact, a browser game about spacecraft design, you play a mission control investigator. Inspect the spacecraft, reconstruct its last hours from the flight recorder, and work out what failed. Then redesign the mission and test whether your change keeps the spacecraft alive long enough to deliver its science.

The full campaign is designed around eight investigations. Three are playable in the current build, and we’re completing the remaining five for the hackathon release.

Why we built it

Students can learn how solar panels, batteries, and radios work individually and still have little practice managing them together. Transmitting more often lets a mission return more observations and increases its need for power and ground-station time. We built Last Contact so players can change one decision, see its effect across the mission, and explain why a design succeeds or fails.

How the game works

Each investigation starts with an assigned mission objective and a baseline spacecraft. Players decide what to change within the mission’s constraints, run the redesigned flight through its operating period or maneuver window, and check whether the result meets the objective.

  1. Intercept the last transmission. A narrated reconstruction introduces the spacecraft, its objective, and the moment something goes wrong.
  2. Investigate the flight. Explore the orbit and the 3D spacecraft. Select evidence markers and move through the flight recorder to see what the spacecraft was doing before contact was lost.
  3. Decode the evidence. Put the recovered measurements into an equation on the theory board. Check the result against the recorder, then identify the cause of the failure.
  4. Redesign the mission. Preview a hardware, orbit, software, or communications change, depending on the case. Examine the updated resource gauges and predict what will happen before committing to a test.
  5. Verify the result. Compare the new flight with the original flight. The case report tracks whether the spacecraft survived, met its science objective, and stayed within the case’s target for design cost. Filing a report after saving a spacecraft unlocks the next case.

Mission design lessons grounded in NASA resources

We drew on spacecraft specifications, engineering references, and anomaly reports to build the investigations. The Science notes in the playable build link to the original sources and identify the values we chose for the exercises. The game simulates flight telemetry from those settings.

Power across an orbit

Mission objective. Keep the satellite operating for 365 simulated days and return at least 90% of the planned science data.

The fictional solar X-ray satellite in the opening investigation is modeled on the scale of MinXSS, a real 3U CubeSat. We use the MinXSS team’s published 25 W peak load as the spacecraft’s default load during a radio pass. Players investigate whether the energy collected in sunlight can support the satellite through the entire orbit, including time spent in Earth’s shadow. (MinXSS mission presentation and NASA Small Spacecraft Power Subsystems)

On an orbit without a radio pass, the player combines panel output, sunlight duration, and continuous spacecraft load. The theory board shows a loss of 1.24 watt-hours using the model’s full-precision values. That matches the simulated recorder. The result explains why starting with a full battery only delays the loss of contact if the spacecraft continues spending more energy than it collects.

In one redesign, deployable solar wings raise the modeled output in sunlight from 12.1 W to 27.1 W and add 0.36 kg to the design. The spacecraft survives the flight and delivers 51% of the planned science data. The next test adds a radio pass every orbit. That uses more radio energy and ground-station time and raises simulated science delivery to 100%. The combined redesign scores 45 design cost points against a target of 70 or fewer. Players can also test whether another launch date and orbital plane give the existing panels more time in sunlight.

Onboard storage and data delivery

Mission objective. Keep the camera satellite operating for 120 simulated days and return at least 35% of its planned science data.

NASA documented how a flash file-system problem on the Spirit rover exhausted available memory and caused repeated resets. Our fictional camera satellite models a related failure using a recorder that fills faster than the radio can empty it. Players can pause image collection before the recorder fills, then adjust contact time to return enough science. The case makes players distinguish the first fault from the battery loss they eventually see in the recorder. (NASA Spirit Flash Memory Anomaly, Lesson 1483)

Propulsion and shared points of failure

Mission objective. Keep the spacecraft powered and gain at least 300 m/s of velocity change before the 12-hour lunar capture window closes. The modeled science objective requires additional velocity change beyond capture.

NASA/JPL’s report of a lunar CubeSat that fell short of the thrust needed to enter its intended orbit informed this investigation. The game uses the spacecraft’s published 55 W solar-array design figure and models a propellant restriction affecting all four thrusters through a shared feed line. Players estimate the change in velocity the spacecraft can achieve before its capture window closes. They can test hypothetical prelaunch changes such as isolating the affected line or giving thrusters dedicated lines. The game sets the restriction and capture window for the exercise. (NASA/JPL mission outcome and NASA lunar mission design study)

Expected outcomes for the five investigations in development

Backup communications. Salvage useful science data after the primary antenna fails. Players learn to weigh which observations to prioritize or compress when a slower backup link limits what they can send home. (JPL study on recovering a communications link)

Telescope pointing. Keep the telescope steady enough to continue observations after two reaction wheels fail. Players learn how changing the spacecraft’s orientation can balance pressure from sunlight and how pointing constraints affect target choice and fuel use. (JPL spacecraft pointing analysis)

Thermal recovery. Restore stable Sun pointing and bring the spacecraft back into operation. Players learn to trace how lost solar power and frozen propellant compound the failure, then decide which systems need power and heat first. (NASA and ESA spacecraft recovery diary)

Unit checks. Catch and correct an impulse unit mismatch so a maneuver stays on its intended trajectory. Players learn to check the units at the point where one system hands a value to another. (NASA mishap investigation report)

Command validation. Catch an invalid setting before upload to preserve safe pointing, protect the battery, and maintain contact. Players learn how one configuration error can affect orientation, temperature, and communications. (NASA/JPL findings on commands and spacecraft loss)

Design choices and technical implementation

We made the failure investigation part of the engineering task. The clues players find provide the measurements they need to build a theory. The redesigned flight then tests their prediction using the same simulation rules. Previews are free, while each round offers three flight tests, with one change per test. Multiple designs can meet the same objective, so players can compare tradeoffs such as mass, hardware cost, ground contact time, and added mechanism risk. Those costs are game values used to compare decisions.

We built Last Contact with TypeScript, React, Three.js, and Vite. Three.js renders the orbit and spacecraft views with WebGL. The TypeScript engine advances the teaching model in 20-second steps, giving the same result for the same setup. A Web Worker can run flight tests in the background to keep the interface responsive. The current automated suite passed 56 tests in Vitest, covering repeatability, resource accounting, and reference designs for the three playable investigations. The game runs in a browser and saves progress on the current device. Web Audio handles playback and telemetry sound, with prerecorded narration and other audio produced using ElevenLabs.

We simplified the model so players can trace results back to their choices. The power and data-delivery examples use circular Earth orbits and a cylindrical shadow. Added hardware mass affects the design score, and the Earth-orbit model keeps the launch trajectory fixed. Captions, mute, reduced motion, and keyboard controls help learners use the game in different settings. Facilitators can unlock available investigations directly for a lesson.

Intended impact

Last Contact is designed for students, science clubs, and educators who want a short activity about spacecraft systems. Learners can practice reading telemetry, making a prediction from evidence, and explaining the cost of a change. A class can compare two solutions to the same case and discuss which limited resource each solution uses.

Our next step is a learner pilot. We would give participants a short mission problem before play, then ask them to explain a different tradeoff afterward. For example, can they predict when a larger battery only delays failure and identify a change that would close the energy budget? The activity is designed to develop that reasoning, and the pilot would test whether learners can apply it to a new mission.
